ctx.x: Some of them played baseball. I know Harry James had a team and like his band.
Well, like I said, in those days, most all the bands had some sort of outdoor activity that they would like to do. Basie's men, what about Basie?
They didn't try to remember being in baseball.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: He was responsible for Con Basie's theme song, One O'Clock Jump. He wrote that and Basie went ahead and like the other people done, just went ahead and said, it's his number, but it's actually Buster Smith song. I didn't know.

ctx.x: When you once told me there was a Buster Biel in Texas, it was not the same guy that was with Henderson. No, it was different. That may be the same name. I just wondered if he used strange harmonies or Buster Smith, you know, they compare him with Charlie Parker and all that.

Well, not that type of playing, no, but he was a fantastic musician as far as tonation and knowing his instrument because he could also do good arranging. He was responsible for Con Basie's theme song, One O'Clock Jump. He wrote that and Basie went ahead and like the other people done, just went ahead and said, it's his number, but it's actually Buster Smith song. I didn't know. That's right. Well, I see in those days, Con Basie was around there with the Blue Devils. Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland…

Okay, it's going on the third real of Don Alba. It's August the 6th, 1973. Day after your birthday, huh? Day after your birthday, that's right. Let me see, we were talking back there about Buster Smith and all that. What about Chalk? Did I ever ask you about Chalk? Drinking Chalk? Did you ever hear of that? Chalk houses?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: Con Basis stayed in so for me. He just remained with his big band.

ctx.x: How many times did your band break up? One time.

Only one time it really broke up. It really broke up. That was here when I just got tired. Being in just Jit by everybody and I pulled a bus up here on Euro Street where my wife was born. And that's where this Chauncey Holland came and asked me to revive my band and he got to binge it for you to finance it. And that was the only time until I actually gave it up in 1940. Maybe it was another mistake. Because two years later, well possibly not two years, there was another boom come up. Con Basis stayed in so for…
Yeah, I've asked you about it.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: And of course, from there came the Count Basie band.

ctx.x: What bands were famous for their riffs then?

Well, most all bands. All of them set their riffs. The Blue Devils, which was Ben and Morton's band, great riff band. And of course, from there came the Count Basie band. And you had Lansford, my band, Andy Craig, T Holder, Troy Floyd, Trent. Now Trent was a little more sophisticated band, something on the P-Rong style band. Played mostly the high class hotels and schools and colleges in those days. But they also played a lot of gigs, outside gigs. It was one of these real fine, classy bands, Trent was. Troy was…
I know some of the guys that work for C.G. Khan, and maybe we should ask them.
